name: Pale Lumiere Green
lede: Pale Lumiere Green is a soft greenish yellow, the pale tone Robert Ridgway charted beside the parent color Lumiere Green in his 1912 color atlas.

sections.title: A pale tone of Lumiere Green
sections.body:
Pale Lumiere Green puts Ridgway's tone word Pale in front of [[lumiere-green]], one of the paired tone variants his 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* set beside each named hue [1]. Lumiere Green itself is Ridgway's plate XVII, hue 29 prime, tone b, later filed by the ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955 in block 119, and Maerz and Paul's 1930 *Dictionary of Color* lists it as first recorded in 1905 [1].

Its nearest named neighbor is [[pale-veronese-green]], only 2.6 units off and close enough on screen to read as the same color [1]; [[pale-goldenrod]] and [[pale-yellow-green]] each sit 3.2 units away [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds this color in 158 of 23,781 paintings, 0.66 percent, as photographed; narrowing to at least five percent coverage inside a painting leaves 97 [2]. That makes it more common than 58 percent of the named colors in our library [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 0.8 percent of the 1,674 paintings from that century, 2.2 times the archive's overall rate [2]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light, in 70 percent of its 97 appearances by lightness rank [2].

The earliest match dates to 1413, in a work attributed to Oguri Sotan, a floor and not a first since the archive's early centuries are thin; that is 499 years before the name's 1912 record, so the match marks a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not a surviving pigment [2]. Jacob Maris used it most, in 4 of his 40 paintings here, 4.9 times the rate of the museums those works come from [2].
